    62	  // ==== heap allocation (constructed lists become objects) ==================
    63	  // Cons-form emission with a freshness guard (the heap-list-probe discipline:
    64	  // an update-form H[N <- _] never re-normalizes symbolically). heapLoc is
    65	  // monotonic — it does NOT wind back at #pop: returned lists escape by ref.
    66	  // A bare list(VS) Val stays legal (read-only inputs in claims flow unboxed);
    67	  // only CONSTRUCTORS in program syntax allocate.
    68	  syntax Bool ::= isRefV(Val) [function, total]
    69	  rule isRefV(ref(_:Int)) => true
    70	  rule isRefV(_:Val)      => false [owise]
    71	
    72	  // closure cells (Python-faithful capture): the heap holds cellV(V); a
    73	  // cellRef surfacing as the k-redex reads through (lookup is the only use —
    74	  // cellRefs never escape to user-visible values)
    75	  syntax HeapVal ::= cellV(Val)
    76	  syntax Bool ::= isCellRef(Val) [function, total]
    77	  rule isCellRef(cellRef(_:Int)) => true
    78	  rule isCellRef(_:Val)          => false [owise]
    79	  // k-top deref for cell-bound reads surfacing INSIDE the annotated frame
    80	  // (AugAssign's in-place read and friends). The "$cells" guard keeps this
    81	  // DECIDABLY inapplicable in plain frames — an unguarded rule lets the
    82	  // prover narrow abstract k-top values into cellRef junk (probed on
    83	  // 26-remove-duplicates). Cross-frame reads (a comprehension closure
    84	  // reading the enclosing function's cellvar) deref inside #look instead.
    85	  rule <k> cellRef(H:Int) => V ... </k>
    86	       <env> L:Int </env>
    87	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map, _) ... </scopes>
    88	       <heap> ... H |-> cellV(V:Val) ... </heap>
    89	       requires "$cells" in_keys(M)
    90	       [priority(40)]

   106	  syntax Val ::= cellsMark(ParamNames)
   107	  syntax ParamNames ::= cellsOf(Val) [function]

   109	  syntax Bool ::= pnMember(String, ParamNames) [function, total]

   130	  syntax KItem ::= #look(String, Int)
   131	  rule <k> Name(X:String) => #look(X, L) ... </k> <env> L:Int </env>
   132	  rule <k> #look(X:String, L:Int) => {M[X]}:>Val ... </k>
   133	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map, _:Parent) ... </scopes>

   135	  // a SYNTACTICALLY cell-bound name reads through the heap cell AT THE
   136	  // LOOKUP (higher priority beats the plain return above on concrete cell
   137	  // bindings; abstract claim values take the plain rule unchanged) — this
   138	  // covers cross-frame cell reads (a comprehension closure reading the
   139	  // enclosing function's cellvar) without a narrowing-prone k-top redex
   140	  // guarded on the FOUND frame's DECLARED cellvars (pnMember over the

   143	  // drags a narrowing cellV heap match along (probed on 5-intersperse and
   144	  // Q4's abstract `numbers` in the annotated frame)

   150	        andBool {M[X]}:>Val ==K cellRef(H)
   151	       [priority(40)]

   153	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map, parent(P:Int)) ... </scopes>
   154	       requires notBool (X in_keys(M))

   185	  syntax ApplyK ::= toCall(Val)

    50	  rule deepEqV(A:Val, B:Val, _:Map) => A ==K B [owise]
    51	
    52	  // ==== mutator: xs.append(v) — an in-place heap write ======================
    53	  rule <k> #applyK(toCall(boundMethodV(ref(H:Int), "append")), (V:Val, .Vals)) => noneV ... </k>
    54	       <heap> ... H |-> list(VS:ValSeq => valSeqConcat(VS, vCons(V, .ValSeq))) ... </heap>
    55	       [priority(40)]
    56	
    57	  // ==== `x in list` — a <k>-cell fold over #iterNext ========================
    58	  syntax KItem ::= #memberAcc(Val, Iterable) | #memberCont(Val) | "#notB"
    59	  rule <k> Compare(LV:Val, CmpOp("in",     list(VS:ValSeq))) => #memberAcc(LV, list(VS)) ... </k>
    60	  rule <k> Compare(LV:Val, CmpOp("not in", list(VS:ValSeq))) => #memberAcc(LV, list(VS)) ~> #notB ... </k>
    61	  rule <k> #memberAcc(V:Val, IT:Iterable) => #iterNext(IT) ~> #memberCont(V) ... </k>
    62	  rule <k> #iterDone ~> #memberCont(_V:Val) => false ... </k>
    63	  rule <k> #iterYield(E:Val, _:Iterable) ~> #memberCont(V:Val) => true ... </k>
    64	       requires E ==K V
    65	  rule <k> #iterYield(E:Val, R:Iterable) ~> #memberCont(V:Val) => #memberAcc(V, R) ... </k>
    66	       requires notBool (E ==K V)
    67	  rule <k> B:Bool ~> #notB => notBool B ... </k>
    68	endmodule

   109	  rule replaceC(iCons(C:Int, R:IntSeq), A:Int, B:Int) => iCons(C, replaceC(R, A, B)) requires notBool (C ==Int A)

     1	// reference/src/semantics/str.k — MPY-STR
     2	
     3	module MPY-STR
     4	  imports MPY-CORE
     5	  imports MPY-ITER
     6	
     7	  // ==== iteration (the iterator protocol's str case; yields 1-char strings) ==
     8	  rule <k> #iterNext(str(.IntSeq))                 => #iterDone ... </k>
     9	  rule <k> #iterNext(str(iCons(C:Int, R:IntSeq)))
    10	        => #iterYield(str(iCons(C, .IntSeq)), str(R)) ... </k>
    11	
    12	  // ==== str literal (ASCII-only) ============================================
    13	  syntax IntSeq ::= strToCodes(String) [function]
    14	  rule <k> Str(S:String) => str(strToCodes(S)) ... </k>
    15	  rule strToCodes("") => .IntSeq
    16	  rule strToCodes(S:String) => iCons(ordChar(substrString(S, 0, 1)), strToCodes(substrString(S, 1, lengthString(S))))
    17	    requires S =/=String "" andBool ordChar(substrString(S, 0, 1)) <Int 128
    18	
    19	  // ==== operators: + / == / != / in =========================================
    20	  syntax IntSeq ::= seqConcat(IntSeq, IntSeq) [function, total]
    21	  rule seqConcat(.IntSeq, T:IntSeq)                => T
    22	  rule seqConcat(iCons(I:Int, S:IntSeq), T:IntSeq) => iCons(I, seqConcat(S, T))
    23	
    24	  rule applyBin("+",  str(A:IntSeq), str(B:IntSeq)) => str(seqConcat(A, B))
    25	  rule applyCmp("==", str(A:IntSeq), str(B:IntSeq)) => A ==K B
    26	  rule applyCmp("!=", str(A:IntSeq), str(B:IntSeq)) => notBool (A ==K B)
    27	
    28	  // substring membership: `P in X` iff the code-seq P occurs contiguously in X
    29	  rule applyCmp("in",     str(P:IntSeq), str(X:IntSeq)) => strContains(P, X)
    30	  rule applyCmp("not in", str(P:IntSeq), str(X:IntSeq)) => notBool strContains(P, X)
    31	
    32	  syntax Bool ::= strPrefix(IntSeq, IntSeq) [function, total]
    33	  rule strPrefix(.IntSeq, _:IntSeq)               => true
    34	  rule strPrefix(iCons(_:Int, _:IntSeq), .IntSeq) => false
    35	  rule strPrefix(iCons(A:Int, As:IntSeq), iCons(B:Int, Bs:IntSeq)) => A ==Int B andBool strPrefix(As, Bs)
    36	
    37	  syntax Bool ::= strContains(IntSeq, IntSeq) [function, total]
    38	  rule strContains(P:IntSeq, X:IntSeq) => true  requires strPrefix(P, X)
    39	  rule strContains(P:IntSeq, .IntSeq)  => false requires notBool strPrefix(P, .IntSeq)
    40	  rule strContains(P:IntSeq, iCons(C:Int, Xs:IntSeq)) => strContains(P, Xs)
    41	       requires notBool strPrefix(P, iCons(C, Xs))
    42	
    43	  // ==== lexicographic order: < / <= / > / >= by code point (= Python str order on the code
    44	  // model). strLt reduces on GROUND code-seqs (krun) but is inert/OPAQUE on symbolic ones
    45	  // (a proof's codesProj(V) is an abstract IntSeq — no constructor rule matches), so a symbolic
    46	  // str `<` stays a trusted opaque term the way sortVS / intFloatDiv do. Additive: fires only on
    47	  // str </<=/>/>= comparisons.
    48	  syntax Bool ::= strLt(IntSeq, IntSeq) [function, total]
    49	  rule strLt(.IntSeq, .IntSeq)                => false
    50	  rule strLt(.IntSeq, iCons(_:Int, _:IntSeq)) => true
    51	  rule strLt(iCons(_:Int, _:IntSeq), .IntSeq) => false
    52	  rule strLt(iCons(A:Int, As:IntSeq), iCons(B:Int, Bs:IntSeq)) => true          requires A  <Int B
    53	  rule strLt(iCons(A:Int, As:IntSeq), iCons(B:Int, Bs:IntSeq)) => false         requires A  >Int B
    54	  rule strLt(iCons(A:Int, As:IntSeq), iCons(B:Int, Bs:IntSeq)) => strLt(As, Bs) requires A ==Int B
    55	
    56	  rule applyCmp("<",  str(A:IntSeq), str(B:IntSeq)) => strLt(A, B)
    57	  rule applyCmp(">",  str(A:IntSeq), str(B:IntSeq)) => strLt(B, A)
    58	  rule applyCmp("<=", str(A:IntSeq), str(B:IntSeq)) => notBool strLt(B, A)
    59	  rule applyCmp(">=", str(A:IntSeq), str(B:IntSeq)) => notBool strLt(A, B)
    60	endmodule

     2	// Int cases of the operator dispatch; Python // and % are floored (pyMod).

     4	module MPY-INT
     5	  imports MPY-CORE
     6	
     7	  rule applyUn("-", I:Int) => 0 -Int I
     8	
     9	  rule applyBin("+",  I1:Int, I2:Int) => I1 +Int I2
    10	  // Bool participates in int arithmetic (x += (a == b))
    11	  rule applyBin("+",  I:Int, B:Bool) => I +Int #if B #then 1 #else 0 #fi
    12	  rule applyBin("+",  B:Bool, I:Int) => #if B #then 1 #else 0 #fi +Int I
    13	  rule applyBin("-",  I1:Int, I2:Int) => I1 -Int I2
    14	  rule applyBin("*",  I1:Int, I2:Int) => I1 *Int I2
    15	  rule applyBin("%",  I1:Int, I2:Int) => pyMod(I1, I2)
    16	  rule applyBin("//", I1:Int, I2:Int) => (I1 -Int pyMod(I1, I2)) /Int I2
    17	  rule applyBin("**", I1:Int, I2:Int) => I1 ^Int I2 requires I2 >=Int 0
    18	
    19	  syntax Int ::= pyMod(Int, Int) [function]
    20	  rule pyMod(I1:Int, I2:Int) => ((I1 %Int I2) +Int I2) %Int I2
    21	
    22	  rule applyCmp("<",  I1:Int, I2:Int)   => I1 <Int  I2
    23	  rule applyCmp("<=", I1:Int, I2:Int)   => I1 <=Int I2
    24	  rule applyCmp(">",  I1:Int, I2:Int)   => I1 >Int  I2
    25	  rule applyCmp(">=", I1:Int, I2:Int)   => I1 >=Int I2
    26	  rule applyCmp("==", I1:Int, I2:Int)   => I1 ==Int I2
    27	  rule applyCmp("!=", I1:Int, I2:Int)   => I1 =/=Int I2
    28	endmodule

     1	// reference/src/semantics/operators.k — MPY-OPERATORS
     2	// The operator DISPATCH layer: operands evaluate by strictness (heat/cool over KResult=Val),
     3	// the cooled node hands to applyUn/applyBin/applyCmp (declared in core.k; each domain file
     4	// owns its cases — bool.k, int.k, float.k, str.k, list.k, tuple.k, set.k, dict.k).
     5	
     6	module MPY-OPERATORS
     7	  imports MPY-CORE
     8	  imports MPY-ITER
     9	
    10	  rule <k> UnaryOp(OP:String, V:Val) => applyUn(OP, V) ... </k>
    11	
    12	  rule <k> BinOp(OP:String, L:Val, R:Val) => applyBin(OP, L, R) ... </k>
    13	
    14	  // Compare's right operand sits under the CmpOp wrapper — contexts instead of attributes
    15	  context Compare(HOLE, _)
    16	  context Compare(_:Val, CmpOp(_, HOLE))
    17	  rule <k> Compare(LV:Val, CmpOp(OP:String, RV:Val)) => applyCmp(OP, LV, RV) ... </k> [owise]
    18	
    19	  rule applyCmp("is",     V:Val, noneV) => V ==K noneV
    20	  rule applyCmp("is not", V:Val, noneV) => notBool (V ==K noneV)
    21	
    22	  // ==== operand deref: heap objects combine/compare by STRUCTURE ============
    23	  // (Python: list == is structural; identity only via `is`.) priority(40)
    24	  // preempts the generic dispatch so applyUn/applyBin/applyCmp never see a ref.
    25	  rule <k> BinOp(OP:String, ref(H:Int), R:Expr) => BinOp(OP, V, R) ... </k>
    26	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    27	       [priority(40)]
    28	  rule <k> BinOp(OP:String, L:Val, ref(H:Int)) => BinOp(OP, L, V) ... </k>
    29	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    30	       requires notBool isRefV(L)
    31	       [priority(40)]
    32	
    33	  // the left operand of `in`/`not in` is an ELEMENT (compares by ==K) — never deref'd
    34	  rule <k> Compare(ref(H:Int), CmpOp(OP:String, R:Expr)) => Compare(V, CmpOp(OP, R)) ... </k>
    35	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    36	       requires OP =/=String "in" andBool OP =/=String "not in"
    37	       [priority(40)]
    38	  rule <k> Compare(L:Val, CmpOp(OP:String, ref(H:Int))) => Compare(L, CmpOp(OP, V)) ... </k>
    39	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    40	       requires notBool isRefV(L)
    41	        orBool OP ==String "in" orBool OP ==String "not in"
    42	       [priority(40)]
    43	
    44	  rule <k> UnaryOp(OP:String, ref(H:Int)) => UnaryOp(OP, V) ... </k>
    45	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    46	       [priority(40)]
    47	endmodule

     6	// over a SYMBOLIC dict passes `dictV(KS, WS)` with a symbolic key sequence KS and reads
     7	// `d.keys() = list(KS)`, then keeps each key opaque problem-locally.

    10	// `isinstance(x, int)` rejects it), the `{k: v, ...}` literal, and `.keys()`. More dict ops (subscript
    11	// / `.get()` / `.values()` / dict `==`) are added as dict problems need them — kept minimal + additive.

    16	  imports MPY-METHODS
    17	  imports MPY-LIST

    25	                 | #dictVal(Val, Entries, ValSeq, ValSeq)

    27	  rule <k> #dictAcc(.Entries, KS:ValSeq, VS:ValSeq) => dictV(KS, VS) ... </k>
    28	  rule <k> #dictAcc((Entry(K:Expr, V:Expr), REST:Entries), KS:ValSeq, VS:ValSeq)

     1	// reference/src/semantics/float.k — MPY-FLOAT
     2	//
     3	// Minimal, TRUSTED float support. K/Haskell (kprove) has no usable symbolic IEEE-754 theory and
     4	// no Int2Float hook, so a float value stays an OPAQUE proof-domain primitive: `intFloatDiv(I, F)`
     5	// (the Python true division I / F) is `[no-evaluators]` for kprove — it never reduces on symbolic
     6	// input, and the proof verifies only the STRUCTURE (the result is the exact term the program
     7	// builds). The `[concrete]` rule evaluates it for krun (llvm HAS the Int2Float / /Float hooks), so
     8	// smoke tests run the real float value.
     9	//
    10	// Only the pieces needed so far: Float as a Val, the float literal, and Int / float true division
    11	// (the `a * h / 2.0` idiom). More float ops (float +/-/*, comparison) are added as float problems
    12	// need them — kept minimal + sound.

    14	module MPY-FLOAT

    16	  imports MPY-BUILTINS
    17	  imports FLOAT

    26	
    27	  rule applyBin("/", I:Int, F:Float) => intFloatDiv(I, F)
    28	
    29	  // Int / Int true division (Python: always a float). OPAQUE for kprove; concrete for krun.

    32	  rule applyBin("/", I1:Int, I2:Int) => divII(I1, I2)
    33	
    34	  // float % float (e.g. `number % 1.0` = the fractional part). OPAQUE for kprove, concrete for
    35	  // krun. Python's float `%` is floor-based: a % b = a - floor(a/b)*b (K's %Float is IEEE
    36	  // remainder, which differs — 3.5 %Float 1.0 = -0.5 vs Python 0.5 — so it is NOT used).
    37	  syntax Float ::= floatMod(Float, Float) [function, total, symbol(floatMod), no-evaluators]
    38	  rule floatMod(F1:Float, F2:Float) => F1 -Float (floorFloat(F1 /Float F2) *Float F2) [concrete]
    39	  rule applyBin("%", F1:Float, F2:Float) => floatMod(F1, F2)
    40	
    41	  // float equality — for concrete krun asserts (e.g. `area == 7.5`); the FLOAT.eq hook is fine on
    42	  // concrete floats. kprove proofs return floats structurally and do not compare them.
    43	  rule applyCmp("==", F1:Float, F2:Float) => F1 ==Float F2
    44	  rule applyCmp("!=", F1:Float, F2:Float) => notBool (F1 ==Float F2)

    50	  syntax Bool ::= floatLt(Float, Float) [function, total, symbol(floatLt), no-evaluators]

    52	  rule applyCmp("<", F1:Float, F2:Float) => floatLt(F1, F2)

     1	// reference/src/semantics/set.k — MPY-SET
     2	
     3	module MPY-SET
     4	  imports MPY-CORE
     5	
     6	  // a set value, carried as its distinct codes in first-seen order (order is irrelevant
     7	  // to membership/cardinality — the two observations sets support here).
     8	  syntax Val ::= setV(IntSeq)
     9	
    10	  // membership of a code in the accumulated distinct-code sequence
    11	  syntax Bool ::= codeIn(Int, IntSeq) [function, total]
    12	  rule codeIn(_:Int, .IntSeq)                => false
    13	  rule codeIn(C:Int, iCons(H:Int, T:IntSeq)) => C ==Int H orBool codeIn(C, T)
    14	
    15	  // the distinct codes of CS (insert-if-absent fold, first-seen order)
    16	  syntax IntSeq ::= dedupCodes(IntSeq)         [function, total]
    17	                  | dedupFrom(IntSeq, IntSeq)  [function, total]
    18	  rule dedupCodes(CS:IntSeq) => dedupFrom(CS, .IntSeq)
    19	  rule dedupFrom(.IntSeq, ACC:IntSeq) => ACC
    20	  rule dedupFrom(iCons(C:Int, S:IntSeq), ACC:IntSeq) => dedupFrom(S, ACC)
    21	       requires codeIn(C, ACC)
    22	  rule dedupFrom(iCons(C:Int, S:IntSeq), ACC:IntSeq) => dedupFrom(S, snocCode(ACC, C))
    23	       requires notBool codeIn(C, ACC)
    24	
    25	  syntax IntSeq ::= snocCode(IntSeq, Int) [function, total]
    26	  rule snocCode(.IntSeq, C:Int)                => iCons(C, .IntSeq)
    27	  rule snocCode(iCons(H:Int, T:IntSeq), C:Int) => iCons(H, snocCode(T, C))
    28	
    29	  // ==== set equality: two sets are equal iff mutually subsuming ==============
    30	  // subsetCodes(A, B) — every code of A occurs in B (duplicates in A are harmless).
    31	  syntax Bool ::= subsetCodes(IntSeq, IntSeq) [function, total]
    32	  rule subsetCodes(.IntSeq, _:IntSeq)                => true
    33	  rule subsetCodes(iCons(C:Int, S:IntSeq), B:IntSeq) => codeIn(C, B) andBool subsetCodes(S, B)
    34	
    35	  syntax Bool ::= sameSet(IntSeq, IntSeq) [function, total]
    36	  rule sameSet(A:IntSeq, B:IntSeq) => subsetCodes(A, B) andBool subsetCodes(B, A)
    37	
    38	  // set == set  (the only comparison sets support here)
    39	  rule applyCmp("==", setV(A:IntSeq), setV(B:IntSeq)) => sameSet(A, B)
    40	endmodule

     3	module MPY-SUBSCRIPT
     4	  imports MPY-CORE
     5	
     6	  // ==== positional access + negative-index normalization (used only here) ===
     7	  // valSeqAt is [total]: in-bounds vCons access reduces as usual; on an OPAQUE sequence (e.g.
     8	  // a trusted sort's sortVS(VS)) or OOB it stays an abstract total value — so indexing the
     9	  // opaque sorted list is DEFINED (no undischarged #Ceil), matching the old semantics' total
    10	  // atK. K trusts the [total] annotation; valid programs index in-bounds.
    11	  syntax Val ::= valSeqAt(ValSeq, Int) [function, total]
    12	  rule valSeqAt(vCons(V:Val, _:ValSeq), 0)     => V
    13	  rule valSeqAt(vCons(_:Val, S:ValSeq), I:Int) => valSeqAt(S, I -Int 1)
    14	       requires I >Int 0
    15	
    16	  syntax Int ::= intSeqAt(IntSeq, Int) [function]
    17	  rule intSeqAt(iCons(C:Int, _:IntSeq), 0)     => C
    18	  rule intSeqAt(iCons(_:Int, S:IntSeq), I:Int) => intSeqAt(S, I -Int 1)
    19	       requires I >Int 0
    20	
    21	  syntax Int ::= normIdx(Int, Int) [function, total]
    22	  rule normIdx(I:Int, LEN:Int) => I +Int LEN requires I  <Int 0
    23	  rule normIdx(I:Int, _:Int)   => I          requires I >=Int 0
    24	
    25	  // ==== Subscript: indexing obj[i] (list / tuple / str) =====================
    26	  // contexts (not strict attrs): the Index slot's Slice alternative must never heat
    27	  context Subscript(HOLE, _)
    28	  context Subscript(_:Val, HOLE:Expr)
    29	
    30	  // heap-object deref (covers both the index and slice forms via the Index slot)
    31	  rule <k> Subscript(ref(H:Int), IX:Index) => Subscript(V, IX) ... </k>
    32	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    33	       [priority(40)]
    34	
    35	  rule <k> Subscript(OBJ:Val, I:Int) => applyIndex(OBJ, I) ... </k>
    36	
    37	  syntax Val ::= applyIndex(Val, Int) [function]
    38	  rule applyIndex(list(VS:ValSeq),  I:Int) => valSeqAt(VS, normIdx(I, vsLen(VS)))
    39	  rule applyIndex(tuple(VS:ValSeq), I:Int) => valSeqAt(VS, normIdx(I, vsLen(VS)))
    40	  rule applyIndex(str(IS:IntSeq),   I:Int)
    41	    => str(iCons(intSeqAt(IS, normIdx(I, isLen(IS))), .IntSeq))

    51	  rule <k> #evalB(E:Expr)   => E ~> #toSome ... </k>

    56	  rule <k> HI:OptInt ~> #slHi(OBJ:Val, LO:OptInt, ST:Bound)  => #evalB(ST) ~> #slStep(OBJ, LO, HI) ... </k>

    60	       [priority(45)]
    61	  rule <k> ST:OptInt ~> #slStep(OBJ:Val, LO:OptInt, HI:OptInt) => doSlice(OBJ, LO, HI, ST) ... </k>
    62	
    63	  syntax Val ::= doSlice(Val, OptInt, OptInt, OptInt) [function]
    64	  rule doSlice(list(VS:ValSeq), LO:OptInt, HI:OptInt, ST:OptInt)
    65	    => list(buildVS(VS, slStart(LO, ST, vsLen(VS)), slStop(HI, ST, vsLen(VS)), slStep(ST)))
    66	  rule doSlice(tuple(VS:ValSeq), LO:OptInt, HI:OptInt, ST:OptInt)
    67	    => tuple(buildVS(VS, slStart(LO, ST, vsLen(VS)), slStop(HI, ST, vsLen(VS)), slStep(ST)))

    71	  // ==== slice.indices: step / start / stop / clamp ==========================
    72	  syntax Int ::= slStep(OptInt) [function, total]
    73	  rule slStep(noB)          => 1
    74	  rule slStep(someB(S:Int)) => S

    77	  rule slStart(noB,          ST:OptInt, _LEN:Int) => 0
    78	       requires slStep(ST) >Int 0
    79	  rule slStart(noB,          ST:OptInt, LEN:Int)  => LEN -Int 1

    86	  rule slStop(noB,          ST:OptInt, _LEN:Int) => -1
    87	       requires slStep(ST) <Int 0

    91	  rule slAdjust(I:Int, LEN:Int, STEP:Int) => clampLo(I +Int LEN, STEP)
    92	       requires I  <Int 0
    93	  rule slAdjust(I:Int, LEN:Int, STEP:Int) => clampHi(I, LEN, STEP)

    96	  syntax Int ::= clampLo(Int, Int) [function, total]

    98	       requires J >=Int 0
    99	  rule clampLo(J:Int, STEP:Int)  => #if STEP <Int 0 #then -1 #else 0 #fi

   101	
   102	  syntax Int ::= clampHi(Int, Int, Int) [function, total]
   103	  rule clampHi(I:Int, LEN:Int, _STEP:Int) => I
   104	       requires I  <Int LEN
   105	  rule clampHi(I:Int, LEN:Int, STEP:Int)  => #if STEP <Int 0 #then LEN -Int 1 #else LEN #fi
   106	       requires I >=Int LEN
   107	
   108	  // ==== build the strided sub-sequence (indices in range by construction) ====
   109	  syntax ValSeq ::= buildVS(ValSeq, Int, Int, Int) [function]
   110	  rule buildVS(VS:ValSeq, I:Int, STOP:Int, STEP:Int)
   111	    => vCons(valSeqAt(VS, I), buildVS(VS, I +Int STEP, STOP, STEP))
   112	       requires (STEP >Int 0 andBool I <Int STOP) orBool (STEP <Int 0 andBool I >Int STOP)

   114	       requires notBool ((STEP >Int 0 andBool I <Int STOP) orBool (STEP <Int 0 andBool I >Int STOP))
   115	
   116	  syntax IntSeq ::= buildIS(IntSeq, Int, Int, Int) [function]
   117	  rule buildIS(IS:IntSeq, I:Int, STOP:Int, STEP:Int)
   118	    => iCons(intSeqAt(IS, I), buildIS(IS, I +Int STEP, STOP, STEP))
   119	       requires (STEP >Int 0 andBool I <Int STOP) orBool (STEP <Int 0 andBool I >Int STOP)
   120	  rule buildIS(_:IntSeq, I:Int, STOP:Int, STEP:Int) => .IntSeq
   121	       requires notBool ((STEP >Int 0 andBool I <Int STOP) orBool (STEP <Int 0 andBool I >Int STOP))
   122	endmodule

+#!/usr/bin/env python3
+"""Generate deterministic K-concrete assertions from the trusted CPython oracle."""

+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import importlib.util
+import itertools
+import random

+
+
+def load_entry(path: Path, name: str):
+    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(name, path)
+    assert spec is not None and spec.loader is not None
+    module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
+    spec.loader.exec_module(module)
+    return module.sort_array
+

+    Path("/tmp/audit-work/reconstruction/canonical.py"), "trusted_canonical_for_k"

"""Generate deterministic K-concrete assertions from the trusted CPython oracle."""

from __future__ import annotations

import importlib.util
import itertools
import random
import sys

def load_entry(path: Path, name: str):
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(name, path)
    assert spec is not None and spec.loader is not None
    module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    spec.loader.exec_module(module)
    return module.sort_array


canonical = load_entry(
    Path("/tmp/audit-work/reconstruction/canonical.py"), "trusted_canonical_for_k"

*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: /audit-output/REVIEW.md
+# Independent adversarial review: 116-sort-array
+
+The reconstructed theorem is legitimate but has a material, non-fatal trust
+limitation: it soundly proves that the real translated program returns the
+supplied semantics' opaque `sortKeyVS(sortVS(...), keyClosure)` result, but the
+mounted K theory contains no universal theorem that those opaque symbols mean
+ascending and stable keyed sorting. The boundary is a fixed external Python
+builtin in the supplied semantics, not a candidate-authored oracle or an
+execution-bypassing local rule. The real program, full stated input domain,
+result reference, heap content, and key closure are all constrained and
+non-vacuous. Finite CPython and LLVM evidence supports the external sorting
+contract but does not prove it.
+
+## 1. Input and provenance integrity
+
+The launcher declares `record_layout = legacy-selected-stage1`,
+`semantics_mode = SUPPLIED_SEMANTICS`, problem `116-sort-array`, and condition
+`semantics`. I used the container paths in `/audit-input.json`, not its
+host-only provenance paths.
+
+All layout-required records are present, readable, regular mounted entries:
+
+- `/audit-input.json`, `/audit-campaign-lock.json`, `/run.json`,
+  `/task.json`, and `/generation-result.json`;
+- `/generation-evidence/invocation.json`, `metrics.json`, `codex-last.txt`,
+  `codex-output.log`, `prompt.txt`, and the structured trace;
+- optional `usage.json`, which is present and was inspected;
+- `/reference/canonical.py`, `/reference/prompt.py`,
+  `/reference/py2mpy.py`, and `/reference/reference-semantics`;
+- the complete `/candidate` mount.
+
+Historical runtime metrics are absent, as permitted for this legacy layout; I
+did not reconstruct them. The campaign lock is normalized-JSON identical to
+the `audit_campaign` block and its SHA-256 is the recorded
+`ad5dfcc006af...`. Every directly recorded file hash checked in
+[integrity-check-rerun.log](evidence/stage1/integrity-check-rerun.log) matches,
+including the run/task/result records, generation prompt/log/last/metrics/usage,
+canonical, prompt, translator, and campaign lock.
+
+The trace has one regular JSONL file and 163 structured records. Its individual
+file digest `5b27883f...` matches the generation result and invocation records.
+The independently reproduced pipeline tree digest is `be170771...`, matching
+`usage.json`'s `source_trace_sha256`. The fresh candidate pipeline-tree digest
+is `53cc1c94...`, exactly the retained workspace digest in
+`generation-result.json` and `invocation.json`. The launcher also records
+aggregate hashes made under other provenance conventions; I did not equate
+those with a plain file or pipeline-tree digest. Direct type inspection and
+recursive byte comparison are stronger for the mounted trees here.
+
+The candidate prompt and translator are byte-identical to their trusted mounts.
+The candidate `reference-semantics/` contains no symlinks or unsupported entry
+types and recursively matches `/reference/reference-semantics` with no missing,
+additional, renamed, mistyped, or changed entry. The independently reproduced
+manifest digest for each tree is the recorded
+`4e06397a1c5a...`. The required trusted semantics mount is present, consistent
+with `SUPPLIED_SEMANTICS`. There is no infrastructure breach.
+
+The generation logs and trace were inspected only as untrusted historical
+claims. They report an initial parse failure, later builds, finite tests, and a
+`#Top`; none was reused as proof evidence. Relevant artifacts:
+
+- [mounted-inventory.log](evidence/stage1/mounted-inventory.log)
+- [integrity-check-rerun.log](evidence/stage1/integrity-check-rerun.log)
+- [tree-hashes.log](evidence/stage1/tree-hashes.log)

+- [trace-inspection.log](evidence/stage1/trace-inspection.log)
+- [generation-log-inspection.log](evidence/stage1/generation-log-inspection.log)
+
+Stage 1 result: integrity passes.

## 5. Rule-by-rule static soundness review

The exhaustive source inventory is
[full-rule-inventory.log](evidence/stage5/full-rule-inventory.log). It records
all 1,231 declarations from the assembler, all 23 supplied helper files,
`verification.k`, and `spec.k`, including:

- 704 rules: 238 touching `<k>` and 466 equational;
- 234 syntax records, 153 function declarations, and 114 `total`
  declarations;
- 34 priority, 47 `concrete`, and 29 `owise` rules;
- 25 `symbol` declarations;
- four claims and one configuration;
- zero simplification rules.

[static-assessment.md](evidence/stage5/static-assessment.md) gives a
file-by-file disposition covering every inventory record, then maps every
constructor used by `solution.mpy` to its declaration and operational rules.
The critical path is:

```text
module load -> closure call/frame -> bind arr -> lookup sorted
-> evaluate inner sorted(arr) -> allocate heap 0
-> evaluate exact annotated key lambda
-> outer keyed sorted -> allocate heap 1
-> return ref(1) -> pop frame
```

The helper key path additionally follows integer comparison, complementary
`IfExp` guards, `bin`, string construction, attribute/method binding, and the
terminating `cntSub` scan. Relevant call/return rules preserve environment,
stack, scope, heap allocation, return, exception, and exit cells. Evaluation is
left-to-right. Priority rules used on this path only dereference heap objects
or select the LLVM concrete keyed sorter; their guards and state footprints are
consistent with the operations they preempt.

All nine candidate equations are truthful definitions:

- four exact constructor names for the lambda, function body, closure, and
  module;
- one exact constructor for the evaluated key closure;
- one postcondition abbreviation,
  `sortArraySpec(VS) = sortKeyVS(sortVS(VS), popcountKeyClosure)`;
- three complete, disjoint, structurally recursive equations for
  `allNonNegativeInts`.

They do not match or replace an executing `Call`, have no priority or
simplification attribute, introduce no fresh/opaque value, and do not encode a
different program. Totality is complete over every actual use. The module-load
and key reachability claims supply independent fixed-semantics connections for
the two manually named closures. No candidate rule can enable a concrete false
conclusion on an intended input.

### Supplied opaque sorting boundary

The proof definition intentionally leaves these fixed-semantics symbols
opaque:

```k

sortKeyVS(ValSeq, Val)
```

They are total, result-bearing, `no-evaluators` symbols. The ordinary and keyed
`sorted` rules allocate lists containing them. This is an external primitive
boundary for Python's builtin `sorted`, not a candidate extension and not a
program-defined helper. The theorem is sound under every interpretation: it
claims exactly that execution returns those primitive applications.

The semantic comments say they mean ascending and stable keyed sorting, and
`MPY-CONCRETE` supplies a separate LLVM-only insertion-sort implementation
that calls the real key closure. The ascending insertion rule places a new
element after equal keys, so it is stable. Fresh K execution agrees with
CPython on 85 cases: nine named boundary/large/tie cases, all length-two lists
over `0..5`, and 40 deterministic randomized lists. See
[k-differential-generate-bounded.log](evidence/stage5/k-differential-generate-bounded.log)
and
[k-differential-bounded-krun.log](evidence/stage5/k-differential-bounded-krun.log).

(exit 137), recorded in
[k-differential-krun.log](evidence/stage5/k-differential-krun.log); this
resource failure is not treated as a proof defect or success.

opaque Haskell symbols with the concrete twin or proving ordering, permutation,
stability, and exact key invocation. The separate key claim proves what the
closure computes when called; it does not prove `sortKeyVS` calls it. Finite
tests cannot close that universal gap. Accordingly, the natural-language
ordering conclusion is conditional on the named supplied primitive contract.
This is the reason for `CONCERNS`, rather than `PASS`.

The LLVM compiler reports non-exhaustive total-function patterns for
`mapStrVS`, `floorFI`, `toF`, `ceilF`, `joinCodes`, and `valSeqAt`. None occurs

variables in disjoint `strLt` branches. An inactive reverse-sort branch reverses
the complete concrete sequence and therefore is not a full CPython model of
stability among equal keys under `reverse=True`; the submitted program never
constructs a `reverse` keyword, so no intended-domain input can expose that
branch. I record it as an unused minimal-semantics limitation, not an
unsoundness witness for this theorem.

local oracle, or execution bypass exists. The fixed external sorting opacity
is sound as a conditional boundary but lacks universal validation of its
human-facing meaning.

No candidate `spec-vacuity.k` was relied on. I created two fresh mutations in
scratch and preserved them under `evidence/stage6/`.

changes heap 1 from

```k

```

to the false alternative:

```k

```

pre-sort is `[3,4]`, while the prose rule, canonical, and candidate produce
`[4,3]`. The mutated spec dry run exits 0, establishing successful parsing and
build. Its proof exits 1 with `WarnStuckClaimState`; the residual is precisely

`sortVS(VS)`. It is not a parse error, missing import, timeout, unrelated
crash, or unreachable mutation.

result content.

## 7. Proven versus assumed accounting

### Machine-proven under the supplied theory

- The trusted-regenerated submitted module loads and installs the exact
  `sort_array` closure.
- For every finite list of arbitrary-size non-negative integers, fixed
  symbolic execution of the exact submitted body consumes the call, restores
  normal control/state cells, allocates exactly two result objects, and returns
  the outer object.
- That object's formal content is exactly
  `sortKeyVS(sortVS(VS), popcountKeyClosure)`.
- Executing the exact key closure on every non-negative integer returns the
  count of `"1"` in its fixed-semantics binary representation.
- The candidate's extra negative branch returns key 0 for every negative
  integer.
- The result and body are non-vacuous under both body and postcondition
  mutations.

### Trusted or informal boundaries

| Boundary | Influence | Status and evidence |
|---|---|---|
| `sortVS` supplied primitive | Intermediate decimal ordering and therefore final tie order | External fixed builtin contract; opaque in Haskell. Concrete twin and finite K/Python tests support it, but no universal K connection theorem is mounted. Concerning but not illegitimate. |
| `sortKeyVS` supplied primitive | Entire returned permutation, ordering, stability, and whether/how the key is called | External fixed builtin contract; opaque in Haskell. This is the principal concern. The formal theorem stays conditional and cannot prove an unrelated concrete result. |
| `MPY-CONCRETE` keyed-sort twin | Empirical bridge from executable K behavior to CPython | Real key calls and stable ascending insertion; 85 fresh cases pass. It is a different imported module from the proof definition, so finite agreement is evidence only. |
| Trusted translator | Source-to-constructor identity | Trusted regeneration is byte-identical; independent constructor comparison pins the proof term. Acceptable. |
| Supplied operational subset | Calls, lookup, allocation, closure/frame, integer/string/bin/count behavior | Fixed trusted semantics, reviewed rule-by-rule on the actual path and exercised concretely. No material path discrepancy found. |
| Prose/canonical intent choice | Resolves contradictory displayed examples | The prose domain/order and trusted canonical agree on all in-domain tests; contradictory displays are documented. No domain restriction was introduced. |
| K toolchain/backend | Compiler and prover correctness | Standard trusted verification tool boundary, version recorded, with fresh builds and mutations. |

The candidate's historical prose, traces, previous `#Top`, and differential
tests are not used as substitutes for the reachability proof. The independent
differentials support only source fidelity and the finite concrete bridge.

### Decision

This is not `FAIL`: the proof reconstructs, is non-vacuous and
result-constraining, mechanically pins the real program, and universally
covers the full non-negative-integer-list source domain. It does not prove a
substituted program, bounded sizes, or examples only. No candidate rule enables
a false conclusion.

This is not `PASS`: the central human-facing meaning of the returned opaque
sorting terms has no universal connection theorem in the mounted theory. The
limitation is precisely the kind of fixed external trust/evidence boundary
allowed by `CONCERNS / LEGIT`: the theorem remains sound and conditional and
does not fabricate a concrete answer under an arbitrary interpretation.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Check required review structure, final markers, and local evidence links."""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
from pathlib import Path


root = Path("/audit-output")
review = root / "REVIEW.md"
text = review.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
lines = text.splitlines()

expected_tail = ["VERDICT: CONCERNS", "LEGITIMACY: LEGIT"]
assert lines[-2:] == expected_tail, (lines[-2:], expected_tail)

for stage in range(1, 8):
    assert re.search(rf"^## {stage}\.", text, re.MULTILINE), f"missing stage {stage}"

links = re.findall(r"\]\((evidence/[^)]+)\)", text)
missing = [link for link in links if not (root / link).is_file()]
assert not missing, f"missing linked evidence: {missing}"

print(f"REVIEW_LINES {len(lines)}")
print(f"EVIDENCE_LINKS {len(links)}")
print("MISSING_LINKS 0")
print(f"FINAL_LINE_1 {lines[-2]}")
print(f"FINAL_LINE_2 {lines[-1]}")
